editorial_sections.h2: Where the Euro Sign Comes From
paragraphs: Unlike most currency symbols, which evolved gradually over centuries of handwriting, the euro sign was deliberately designed to order. In 1996, ahead of the currency's 1999 introduction, a small internal team at the European Commission narrowed roughly 30 candidate designs down to two finalists and picked the version now in use, commonly credited to Belgian graphic designer Alain Billiet, though the Commission didn't publicize a single named author for years.

The design references the Greek letter epsilon (Ɛ), a nod to Greece as the historical cradle of European civilization, crossed with two parallel horizontal lines. Those lines echo the double-bar style already used by other stable currency symbols of the era, deliberately chosen to signal steadiness and trust in the new shared currency.

faq.a: It was designed in 1996 by a small internal team at the European Commission, chosen from around 30 concepts. Belgian graphic designer Alain Billiet is widely credited as the lead designer, though the Commission kept the exact authorship low-profile for years.

faq.q: What do the two lines through the euro symbol mean?
faq.a: The shape is based on the Greek letter epsilon (Ɛ), referencing Greece as the birthplace of European civilization, with two parallel horizontal lines added across it, a stability cue borrowed from the double-bar style already used on currency symbols like ¥.

faq.q: How do you type the euro sign on Windows or Mac?
faq.a: On Windows, hold Alt and type 0128 on the numeric keypad (Alt+0128), or use Ctrl+Alt+E on many European keyboard layouts. On Mac, press Option+Shift+2. In HTML, use the entity € or €.
